Appendix A Gauge transformations

A.1 Gauge transformation restoring the symmetries of the kagome lattice

The gauge transformations G:fj,σ†→ei​ϕ​(j)​fj,σ†G:f^{{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma}\rightarrow e^{i\phi(j)}f^{{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma} needed to restore the symmetries of the kagome lattice are shown in Fig. 15, for the case of periodic boundary conditions. As it turns out, the ei​ϕ​(j)e^{i\phi(j)} are simple ±1\pm 1 signs, which changes the hoppings ti,jt_{i,j} connected to site jj. In the case of the antiperiodic boundary condition, the projective symmetries of C6C_{6} and σ\sigma are broken (though they are restored in the thermodynamic limit), and the gauge transformation of the translations should be modified at the boundary, as explained in [78].

A.2 Connection between the DSL ansätze

The DSL ansatz used in [60] with a doubled unit cell is shown in Fig. 16(a). The gauge transformation G:fj,σ†→ei​ϕ​(j)​fj,σ†G:f^{{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma}\rightarrow e^{i\phi(j)}f^{{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma} connecting this ansatz with the one shown in Fig. 1 is complicated by its dependence on the cluster size. As shown in Fig. 16(b), the gauge transformation corresponds to sign changes of the fermionic operators along stripes containing whole 12-site unit cells. If the number of such stripes is even, as in Fig. 16(b), then this gauge transformation is enough to connect the two ansätze. However, when the number of stripes is odd, one has to impose an extra antiperiodic boundary condition, as shown in Fig. 16(a). The effect of the APBC is to change the sign of the hoppings it goes through. All sites are located within one such stripe for the smallest 12-site unit cell in Fig. 16(a). Therefore, no fermionic operator acquires a minus sign, and the APBC alone connects this ansatz to the one shown in Fig. 1.

Appendix B Isomorphy of the 12-site unite cell and the OhO_{h} group

The 12-site unit cell is equivalent to a truncated octahedron (see Fig. 17), and its symmetry group is isomorphic to the OhO_{h} point group. The C2C_{2} in the wallpaper group becomes the inversion ii in OhO_{h} with cyclic permutation (1 10)​(2 5)​(3 9)​(4 7)​(6 12)​(8 11)(1\>10)(2\>5)(3\>9)(4\>7)(6\>12)(8\>11). The glide reflection (1 2 7 8)​(3 12 9 6)​(4 11 10 5)(1\>2\>7\>8)(3\>12\>9\>6)(4\>11\>10\>5) becomes the C4C_{4}, and the (1 2 3)​(5 9 10)​(6 7 11)​(4 8 12)(1\>2\>3)(5\>9\>10)(6\>7\>11)(4\>8\>12) is a threefold rotation C3C_{3} in both cases. The ii, C4C_{4} and C3C_{3} are the generators of the OhO_{h}.

Appendix C Relations between the permutations and the diagonal terms

C.1 Expectation values in the Mott phase

The rotational invariance of an SU(NN) singlet state allows us to express expectation values of an off-diagonal operator using diagonal operators only. For example, the two-site permutation operator 𝒫i,j\mathcal{P}_{i,j} reads

⟨𝒫i,j⟩=N⁡(N+1)​⟨ni,σ​nj,σ⟩−1\langle\mathcal{P}_{i,j}\rangle=N(N+1)\langle n_{i,\sigma}n_{j,\sigma}\rangle-1 (39)

and

⟨𝐓i⋅𝐓j⟩=(N+1)​N2​(⟨ni,σ​nj,σ⟩−1N2),\langle\mathbf{T}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{j}\rangle=\frac{(N+1)N}{2}\left(\langle n_{i,\sigma}n_{j,\sigma}\rangle-\frac{1}{N^{2}}\right), (40)

where ⟨ni,σ​nj,σ⟩\langle n_{i,\sigma}n_{j,\sigma}\rangle is the expectation value of the density-density operator of a single flavor σ\sigma. These expressions are instrumental as calculating diagonal matrix elements is much faster in the variational Monte Carlo method than off-diagonal ones.

We also evaluated the expectation values of the three-site terms and density correlations for a few examples of singlet wave functions for different values of NN and sites. By inspection, we arrived at the

⟨𝒫i,j,k+𝒫i,k,j⟩=N2​p3−N​p21+p111+1\langle\mathcal{P}_{i,j,k}+\mathcal{P}_{i,k,j}\rangle=N^{2}p_{3}-Np_{21}+p_{111}+1 (41)

expression, where p3=∑σ⟨ni,σ​nj,σ​nσ,k⟩p_{3}=\sum_{\sigma}\langle n_{i,\sigma}n_{j,\sigma}n_{\sigma,k}\rangle is the probability that the three sites are occupied with the same flavors, p111=∑σ≠σ′≠σ′′⟨ni,σ​nσ′,j​nσ′′,k⟩p_{111}=\sum_{\sigma\neq\sigma^{\prime}\neq\sigma^{\prime\prime}}\langle n_{i,\sigma}n_{\sigma^{\prime},j}n_{\sigma^{\prime\prime},k}\rangle if they are all different, and p21p_{21} if there are precisely two identical flavors, satisfying p3+p21+p111=1p_{3}+p_{21}+p_{111}=1.

We can check Eq. (41) in the following limiting cases: (i) If all three sites are in a fully antisymmetrical NN-site SU(NN) singlet, then ⟨𝒫i,j,k+𝒫i,k,j⟩=2\langle\mathcal{P}_{i,j,k}+\mathcal{P}_{i,k,j}\rangle=2. At the same time, there are no two sites with the same color within the singlet, so p3=p2,1=0p_{3}=p_{2,1}=0 and p111=1p_{111}=1, fulfilling Eq. (41). (ii) If the three sites belong to three disjunct singlets, we get contribution only if they are occupied with the same colors, having probability 1/N31/N^{3}, but since any of the NN colors will do it, ⟨𝒫i,j,k+𝒫i,k,j⟩=2​N×1/N3=2/N2\langle\mathcal{P}_{i,j,k}+\mathcal{P}_{i,k,j}\rangle=2N\times 1/N^{3}=2/N^{2}. The density correlations are also easy to calculate,

p3\displaystyle p_{3} =N​1N3=1N2,\displaystyle=N\frac{1}{N^{3}}=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\;, (42)
p21\displaystyle p_{21} =3​N​(N−1)​1N3=3N−3N2,\displaystyle=3N(N-1)\frac{1}{N^{3}}=\frac{3}{N}-\frac{3}{N^{2}}\;, (43)
p111\displaystyle p_{111} =N⁡(N−1)​(N−2)​1N3=1−3N+2N2.\displaystyle=N(N-1)(N-2)\frac{1}{N^{3}}=1-\frac{3}{N}+\frac{2}{N^{2}}\;. (44)

In this case, we also satisfy Eqs. (41).

C.1.1 Monte Carlo sampling

We use a Monte Carlo method to evaluate the expectation values of different operators in a Gutzwiller projected Fermi sea [89]. First, we express the ⟨𝒫i,j⟩\langle\mathcal{P}_{i,j}\rangle and ⟨𝒫i,j,k+𝒫i,k,j⟩\langle\mathcal{P}_{i,j,k}+\mathcal{P}_{i,k,j}\rangle with the diagonal operators ni,σn_{i,\sigma}, p3p_{3}, p21p_{21} and p111p_{111} using Eqs. (39) and (41). Then, the expectation values of diagonal operators can be easily calculated with Monte Carlo sampling of fermionic configurations. For example,

⟨FS|PG​ni​nj​PG|FS⟩==∑x⟨x​|ni​|x⟩​⟨x|nj|x⟩|​⟨x​|PG|​FS⟩|2,\langle\text{FS}|P_{\text{G}}n_{i}n_{j}P_{\text{G}}|\text{FS}\rangle=\\ =\sum_{x}\langle x|n_{i}|x\rangle\langle x|n_{j}|x\rangle|\langle x|P_{\text{G}}|\text{FS}\rangle|^{2}, (45)

where we inserted the identity operator ∑x|x⟩​⟨x|\sum_{x}|x\rangle\langle x| and the configurations |x⟩|x\rangle runs over all the possible product states of the fermions in real space. We can use P⁡(x)∝|⟨x|PG|FS⟩|2P(x)\propto|\langle x|P_{\text{G}}|\text{FS}\rangle|^{2} as a probability distribution (since the Monte Carlo steps follow each other in a Markov chain, there is no need to impose ∑xP⁡(x)=1\sum_{x}P(x)=1). The effect of the Gutzwiller projector is to select configurations |x⟩|x\rangle with singly occupied sites exclusively. Furthermore, as the PG​|FS⟩P_{\text{G}}|\text{FS}\rangle is an SU(NN) singlet, the configurations giving non-zero contribution have an equal number of flavors. For example, in a 6-site system, there are 6! = 720 such configurations, |x⟩∈{|A,B,C,D,E,F⟩,|B,A,C,D,E,F⟩,…}|x\rangle\in\{|A,B,C,D,E,F\rangle,|B,A,C,D,E,F\rangle,\dots\}. For a system with Ns=6​MsN_{s}=6M_{s} sites, the number of such configurations is Ns!/(Ms!)6N_{s}!/(M_{s}!)^{6}. In the evaluation of the |⟨x|PG|FS⟩|2|\langle x|P_{\text{G}}|\text{FS}\rangle|^{2} we use the standard determinant updates using the Sherman-Morrison formula, see Ref. 8.

Every Monte Carlo step involves many elementary steps corresponding to the correlation time of the given system size. Following the thermalization, we made 1,5×1081,5\times 10^{8} Monte Carlo steps for the SVMC​(𝐤)S_{\text{VMC}}(\mathbf{k}) of the 768-site cluster in Fig. 11(a), 2.5×1072.5\times 10^{7} for the 192-site David star ansatz in the stereographic map in Fig. 7 (with a total of 5703 points), and 4×1094\times 10^{9} for the real-valued perturbations of the DSL in Figs. 5 and 6, with 192-site clusters.

The Monte Carlo sampling of the Hamiltonian and overlap matrices for the calculation of the dynamical structure factor SVMC33​(𝐤,ω)S^{33}_{\text{VMC}}(\mathbf{k},\omega) of a 48-site cluster was explained in detail in Ref. [77], and involved 1.5×1091.5\times 10^{9} Monte Carlo steps, with which the error became negligible.

In the case of the chiral and staggered ansätze in Fig. 9 and in Tab. 4, we performed 10610^{6} Monte Carlo steps separated with 4​Ns4N_{s} elementary steps. For the DSL in the insets of Fig. 9, we increased the number of steps to 8×1068\times 10^{6}.

C.2 Expectation values in the mean-field approximation

For free fermions, the relationship between the exchange of fermions

𝒫i,j=∑σ,σ′fi,σ′†​fj,σ†​fj,σ′​fi,σ\mathcal{P}_{i,j}=\sum_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}f^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma^{\prime}}f^{\dagger}_{j,\sigma}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma^{\prime}}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\sigma} (46)

and 𝐓i⋅𝐓j\mathbf{T}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{j}, where Eq. (3) defines 𝐓i\mathbf{T}_{i}, modifies to

𝒫i,j=2​𝐓i⋅𝐓j+1N​n^i​n^j.\mathcal{P}_{i,j}=2\mathbf{T}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{j}+\frac{1}{N}\hat{n}_{i}\hat{n}_{j}\,. (47)

This follows from Eq. (3) when we take into account that

∑a=1N2−1λα​βa​λμ​νa=2​δα,ν​δμ,β−2N​δα​β​δμ​ν\sum_{a=1}^{N^{2}-1}\lambda^{a}_{\alpha\beta}\lambda^{a}_{\mu\nu}=2\delta_{\alpha,\nu}\delta_{\mu,\beta}-\frac{2}{N}\delta_{\alpha\beta}\delta_{\mu\nu} (48)

for the SU(NN) generalizations of the Gell-Mann matrices [27]. In the fundamental representation n^i=1\hat{n}_{i}=1, we recover Eq. (20).

We shall be careful when we compare the noninteracting expectation values to the projected ones, as they include charge fluctuations. We can use Wick’s theorem to calculate the expectation values:

⟨𝒫i,j⟩′\displaystyle\langle\mathcal{P}_{i,j}\rangle^{\prime} =∑σ,σ′⟨fi,σ†​fj,σ′†​fj,σ​fi,σ′⟩′\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}\langle f^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}f^{\dagger}_{j,\sigma^{\prime}}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle^{\prime}
=∑σ,σ′(⟨fi,σ†​fi,σ′⟩′​⟨fj,σ′†​fj,σ⟩′−⟨fi,σ†​fj,σ⟩′​⟨fj,σ′†​fi,σ′⟩′)\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}\left(\langle f^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle^{\prime}\langle f^{\dagger}_{j,\sigma^{\prime}}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma}\rangle^{\prime}-\langle f^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma}\rangle^{\prime}\langle f^{\dagger}_{j,\sigma^{\prime}}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle^{\prime}\right)
=N​⟨fi†​fi⟩′​⟨fj†​fj⟩′−N2​|⟨fi†​fj⟩′|2\displaystyle=N\langle f^{\dagger}_{i}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\rangle^{\prime}\langle f^{\dagger}_{j}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j}\rangle^{\prime}-N^{2}\left|\langle f^{\dagger}_{i}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j}\rangle^{\prime}\right|^{2}
=1N−N2​|⟨fi†​fj⟩′|2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}-N^{2}|\langle f^{\dagger}_{i}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j}\rangle^{\prime}|^{2}\;, (49)

where we introduced the ⟨FS|A^|FS⟩=⟨A^⟩′\langle\text{FS}|\hat{A}|\text{FS}\rangle=\langle\hat{A}\rangle^{\prime} shorthand notation for the expectation values in the Fermi sea. Furthermore, ⟨fi,σ†​fi,σ′⟩′=δσ,σ′/N\langle f^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\sigma^{\prime}}\rangle^{\prime}=\delta_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}/N in the fundamental representation and ⟨fi†​fj⟩′\langle f^{\dagger}_{i}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j}\rangle^{\prime} denotes ⟨fi,σ†​fj,σ⟩′\langle f^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma}\rangle^{\prime} that is independent of σ\sigma in a singlet (closed shell) Fermi sea. Similarly,

⟨𝐓i⋅𝐓j⟩′\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{T}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{j}\rangle^{\prime} =12​⟨𝒫i,j⟩′−12​N​⟨n^i​n^j⟩′\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\langle\mathcal{P}_{i,j}\rangle^{\prime}-\frac{1}{2}{N}\langle\hat{n}_{i}\hat{n}_{j}\rangle^{\prime}
=−N2−12​|⟨fi†​fj⟩′|2.\displaystyle=-\frac{N^{2}-1}{2}|\langle f^{\dagger}_{i}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j}\rangle^{\prime}|^{2}\,. (50)

Let us also calculate the expectation value of having two fermions of the same flavor on neighboring sites:

⟨n^i,σ​n^j,σ⟩′=1N2−|⟨fi†​fj⟩′|2.\langle\hat{n}_{i,\sigma}\hat{n}_{j,\sigma}\rangle^{\prime}=\frac{1}{N^{2}}-|\langle f^{\dagger}_{i}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j}\rangle^{\prime}|^{2}\;. (51)

We can associate |⟨fi†​fj⟩′|2|\langle f^{\dagger}_{i}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j}\rangle^{\prime}|^{2} with the exchange hole. Since n^i,σ​n^j,σ=(fi,σ​fj,σ)†​fi,σ​fj,σ\hat{n}_{i,\sigma}\hat{n}_{j,\sigma}=(f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\sigma}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma})^{\dagger}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\sigma}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma} is a positive semidefinite operator, we find that the ⟨fi,σ†​fj,σ⟩′\langle f^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma}\rangle^{\prime} is bounded as

|⟨fi,σ†​fj,σ⟩′|≤1N.|\langle f^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma}\rangle^{\prime}|\leq\frac{1}{N}\;. (52)

On one hand, the flavor-flavor correlations are absent in the absence of the exchange hole, so that ⟨𝐓i⋅𝐓j⟩′=0\langle\mathbf{T}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{j}\rangle^{\prime}=0 for |⟨fi,σ†​fj,σ⟩′|=0|\langle f^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma}\rangle^{\prime}|=0. On the other hand, for maximally entangled fermions with |⟨fi,σ†​fj,σ⟩′|=1N|\langle f^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma}\rangle^{\prime}|=\frac{1}{N} we get ⟨𝐓i⋅𝐓j⟩′=−N2−12​N2\langle\mathbf{T}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{j}\rangle^{\prime}=-\frac{N^{2}-1}{2N^{2}}, instead of the ⟨𝐓i⋅𝐓j⟩=−N+12​N\langle\mathbf{T}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{j}\rangle=-\frac{N+1}{2N}, the minimal value which can be achieved within an SU(NN) singlet. So we can approximate

⟨𝐓i⋅𝐓j⟩≈N(N−1)​⟨𝐓i⋅𝐓j⟩′,\langle\mathbf{T}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{j}\rangle\approx\frac{N}{(N-1)}\langle\mathbf{T}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{j}\rangle^{\prime}\;, (53)

which we will refer to as the corrected mean field. This result is analogous to the relation of the Casimir operators ⟨𝐓i⋅𝐓i⟩=N(N−1)​⟨𝐓i⋅𝐓i⟩′\langle\mathbf{T}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{i}\rangle=\frac{N}{(N-1)}\langle\mathbf{T}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{i}\rangle^{\prime} derived in Ref. 78.

For the 3-site ring exchange on a triangle, we get

⟨𝒫123⟩′=⟨f1,α†​f2,γ†​f3,β†​f3,α​f2,β​f1,γ⟩′=N3​|ξ|3​ei​ϕ+N⁡(|ξ|3​e−i​ϕ−3​|ξ|2)+1N2\langle\mathcal{P}_{123}\rangle^{\prime}=\langle f^{\dagger}_{1,\alpha}f^{\dagger}_{2,\gamma}f^{\dagger}_{3,\beta}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{3,\alpha}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2,\beta}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1,\gamma}\rangle^{\prime}=\\ N^{3}|\xi|^{3}e^{i\phi}+N(|\xi|^{3}e^{-i\phi}-3|\xi|^{2})+\frac{1}{N^{2}} (54)

where ξ1,3​ξ3,2​ξ2,1=|ξ|3​ei​ϕ△\xi_{1,3}\xi_{3,2}\xi_{2,1}=|\xi|^{3}e^{i\phi_{\triangle}}. The U(1) gauge invariant ring exchange is thus sensitive to the phase of the ξ\xi’s via their product around the triangle. For ξ=0\xi=0, we get the correct ⟨𝒫123⟩′=1/N2\langle\mathcal{P}_{123}\rangle^{\prime}=1/N^{2}, while for ξ=1/N\xi=1/N it takes the ⟨𝒫123⟩′=(N−1)​(N−2)/N2\langle\mathcal{P}_{123}\rangle^{\prime}=(N-1)(N-2)/N^{2} value instead of 1.

Appendix D Projected mean field

Here, we will closely follow the projected mean-field calculation of Hsu in Ref. 37, where the SU(2) mean-field calculation was extended to enforce single occupancy on nearest neighbor sites only. Below, we summarize the method and extend it to off-diagonal quantities, the SU(NN) case, and three sites when calculating ring exchanges.

D.1 Projected mean field for 2-sites

Let us denote by P⁡(X​Y)P(XY) the probability that site 11 has a flavor XX and site 22 has a flavor YY fermion after Gutzwiller projection. For the SU(66), the flavors are X,Y∈{A,B,…,F}X,Y\in\{A,B,\dots,F\}. We can express the probabilities as

P⁡(A​A)\displaystyle P(AA) =P0(AA)P0(B¯B¯)×⋯×P0(F¯F¯)\displaystyle=P_{0}(AA)P_{0}(\bar{B}\bar{B})\times\cdots\times P_{0}(\bar{F}\bar{F}) (55a)
P⁡(A​B)\displaystyle P(AB) =P0(AA¯)P0(B¯B)P0(C¯C¯)×⋯×P0(F¯F¯)\displaystyle=P_{0}(A\bar{A})P_{0}(\bar{B}B)P_{0}(\bar{C}\bar{C})\phantom{=}\times\cdots\times P_{0}(\bar{F}\bar{F}) (55b)

where P0​(X​X)P_{0}(XX) denotes the probability of finding two fermions of flavor XX at sites 11 and 22 in the Fermi sea before the projection, P0​(X​X¯)P_{0}(X\bar{X}) denotes the probability of finding a fermion with flavor XX at site 11 and not finding it at site 22, and so on (i.e., we denote by X¯\bar{X} the flavor-XX hole, i.e. the absence of that flavor). The product form is the consequence of the fermions of different colors being independent in the Fermi-sea. We can use Wick’s theorem to calculate the probabilities in the Fermi-sea:

P0​(X​X)\displaystyle P_{0}(XX) =⟨n1,X​n2,X⟩′=⟨f1,X†​f1,X​f2,X†​f2,X⟩′\displaystyle=\langle n_{1,X}n_{2,X}\rangle^{\prime}=\langle f^{\dagger}_{1,X}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1,X}f^{\dagger}_{2,X}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2,X}\rangle^{\prime}
=⟨f1,X†​f1,X⟩′​⟨f2,X†​f2,X⟩′−⟨f1,X†​f2,X⟩′​⟨f2,X†​f1,X⟩′\displaystyle=\langle f^{\dagger}_{1,X}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1,X}\rangle^{\prime}\langle f^{\dagger}_{2,X}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2,X}\rangle^{\prime}-\langle f^{\dagger}_{1,X}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2,X}\rangle^{\prime}\langle f^{\dagger}_{2,X}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1,X}\rangle^{\prime}
=|ν1Xξ1,2Xξ2,1Xν2X|=1N2−ξ1,2X​ξ2,1X\displaystyle=\begin{vmatrix}\nu^{X}_{1}&\xi^{X}_{1,2}\\ \xi^{X}_{2,1}&\nu^{X}_{2}\\ \end{vmatrix}=\frac{1}{N^{2}}-\xi^{X}_{1,2}\xi^{X}_{2,1} (56a)
P0​(X​X¯)\displaystyle P_{0}(X\bar{X}) =⟨n1,X​n¯2,X⟩′=|ν1X−ξ1,2Xξ2,1X−ν2X|=N−1N2+ξ1,2X​ξ2,1X\displaystyle=\langle n_{1,X}\bar{n}_{2,X}\rangle^{\prime}=\begin{vmatrix}\nu^{X}_{1}&-\xi^{X}_{1,2}\\ \xi^{X}_{2,1}&1\!-\!\nu^{X}_{2}\\ \end{vmatrix}=\frac{N\!-\!1}{N^{2}}+\xi^{X}_{1,2}\xi^{X}_{2,1} (56b)
P0​(X¯​X¯)\displaystyle P_{0}(\bar{X}\bar{X}) =⟨n¯1,X​n¯2,X⟩′=|−ν1X−ξ1,2X−ξ2,1X−ν2X|\displaystyle=\langle\bar{n}_{1,X}\bar{n}_{2,X}\rangle^{\prime}=\begin{vmatrix}1\!-\!\nu^{X}_{1}&-\xi^{X}_{1,2}\\ -\xi^{X}_{2,1}&1\!-\!\nu^{X}_{2}\\ \end{vmatrix} (56c)
=(N−1)2N2−ξ1,2X​ξ2,1X,\displaystyle=\frac{(N\!-\!1)^{2}}{N^{2}}-\xi^{X}_{1,2}\xi^{X}_{2,1}\;,

where

n¯i,X\displaystyle\bar{n}_{i,X} =1−ni,X,\displaystyle=1-n_{i,X}\,, (57)

and we introduced the νiX≡⟨ni,X⟩′\nu^{X}_{i}\equiv\langle n_{i,X}\rangle^{\prime}, ν¯iX≡⟨n¯i,X⟩′\bar{\nu}^{X}_{i}\equiv\langle\bar{n}_{i,X}\rangle^{\prime} (which take on νiX=1/N\nu^{X}_{i}=1/N and ν¯iX=1−1/N\bar{\nu}^{X}_{i}=1-1/N in a density-uniform state) and the

ξi,jX=⟨fi,X†​fj,X⟩′\xi^{X}_{i,j}=\langle f^{\dagger}_{i,X}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,X}\rangle^{\prime} (58)

off-diagonal expectation values, for which ξi,jX=ξ¯j,iX\xi^{X}_{i,j}=\bar{\xi}^{X}_{j,i} (the bar denotes complex conjugation). These probabilities satisfy the

P0​(X​X)+P0​(X¯​X)+P0​(X​X¯)+P0​(X¯​X¯)=1P_{0}(XX)+P_{0}(\bar{X}X)+P_{0}(X\bar{X})+P_{0}(\bar{X}\bar{X})=1 (59)

condition. We can then approximate the flavor-flavor correlation function by

⟨T13​T23⟩\displaystyle\langle T_{1}^{3}T_{2}^{3}\rangle =14​P⁡(A​A)+P⁡(B​B)−P⁡(A​B)−P⁡(B​A)∑X=AF∑Y=AFP⁡(X​Y)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\frac{P(AA)+P(BB)-P(AB)-P(BA)}{\sum_{X=A}^{F}\sum_{Y=A}^{F}P(XY)}
=14​2​P​(A​A)−2​P​(A​B)N​P​(A​A)+N⁡(N−1)​P​(A​B)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\frac{2P(AA)-2P(AB)}{NP(AA)+N(N-1)P(AB)}
=12​P0​(A​A)​P0​(B¯​B¯)−P0​(A​A¯)​P0​(B¯​B)N​P0​(A​A)​P0​(B¯​B¯)+N⁡(N−1)​P0​(A​A¯)​P0​(B¯​B)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\frac{P_{0}(AA)P_{0}(\bar{B}\bar{B})-P_{0}(A\bar{A})P_{0}(\bar{B}B)}{NP_{0}(AA)P_{0}(\bar{B}\bar{B})+N(N-1)P_{0}(A\bar{A})P_{0}(\bar{B}B)}
=−N2​|ξ|22​[N4​|ξ|4+N3​|ξ|2−2​N2​|ξ|2+(N−1)2].\displaystyle=-\frac{N^{2}|\xi|^{2}}{2\left[N^{4}|\xi|^{4}+N^{3}|\xi|^{2}-2N^{2}|\xi|^{2}+(N-1)^{2}\right]}. (60)

Assuming the full SU(NN) symmetry of the ground state,

⟨𝐓1⋅𝐓2⟩=−(N2−1)​N2​|ξ|22​[N4​|ξ|4+N3​|ξ|2−2​N2​|ξ|2+(N−1)2].\langle\mathbf{T}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{2}\rangle=-\frac{(N^{2}-1)N^{2}|\xi|^{2}}{2\left[N^{4}|\xi|^{4}+N^{3}|\xi|^{2}-2N^{2}|\xi|^{2}+(N-1)^{2}\right]}. (61)

For |ξ|=1/N|\xi|=1/N we recover the expected ⟨𝐓1⋅𝐓2⟩=−N+12​N\langle\mathbf{T}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{2}\rangle=-\frac{N+1}{2N} in a singlet.

Applying the expression above to the SU(2) case, we recover the formula in Ref. 37 by associating the Fermi exchange hole |ξ|2|\xi|^{2} with xx:

⟨𝐒1⋅𝐒2⟩=−6​|ξ|21+16​|ξ|4.\langle\mathbf{S}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{2}\rangle=-\frac{6|\xi|^{2}}{1+16|\xi|^{4}}\,. (62)

The spin-spin correlation function is a monotonically decreasing function of the Fermi exchange hole. It is 0 for the decoupled sites (where |ξ|2=0|\xi|^{2}=0) and takes ⟨𝐒1⋅𝐒2⟩=−3/4\langle\mathbf{S}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{2}\rangle=-3/4 for maximally entangled pair of sites, where |ξ|2=1/2|\xi|^{2}=1/2 is maximal, representing a dimer singlet.

We can generalize the approximation of Hsu to the calculation of expectation values of off-diagonal operators as well, the example being the 𝒫1,2\mathcal{P}_{1,2} transposition (permutation) operator. We calculated the expectation value of 𝒫1,2\mathcal{P}_{1,2} in Eq. (49) in the mean-field approximation. Now we need to distinguish two possible cases: the two sites are either occupied by the same flavor fermions, in which case the 𝒫1,2\mathcal{P}_{1,2} acts trivially as the identity operator, or with different flavors, in which case we cannot use the expressions involving the probabilities P0P_{0}. To overcome this problem, let us introduce the notation ⟨Y​X​|𝒫1,2|​X​Y⟩\langle YX|\mathcal{P}_{1,2}|XY\rangle to denote the amplitude of a process where 𝒫1,2\mathcal{P}_{1,2} exchanges the flavors on sites 11 and 22. For identical flavors (X=YX=Y) the ⟨X​X|𝒫1,2|X​X⟩≡P⁡(X​X)\langle XX|\mathcal{P}_{1,2}|XX\rangle\equiv P(XX) and following Eq. (55a), we can write

⟨X​X|𝒫1,2|X​X⟩=P0​(X​X)​∏Z≠XP0​(Z¯​Z¯).\langle XX|\mathcal{P}_{1,2}|XX\rangle=P_{0}(XX)\prod_{Z\neq X}P_{0}(\bar{Z}\bar{Z}). (63)

For unlike flavors X≠YX\neq Y

⟨Y​X​|𝒫1,2|​X​Y⟩\displaystyle\langle YX|\mathcal{P}_{1,2}|XY\rangle =⟨f1,Y†​f2,X†​f2,Y​f1,X⟩′​∏Z≠X,YP0​(Z¯​Z¯)\displaystyle=\langle f^{\dagger}_{1,Y}f^{\dagger}_{2,X}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2,Y}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1,X}\rangle^{\prime}\prod_{Z\neq X,Y}P_{0}(\bar{Z}\bar{Z})
=−⟨f2,X†f1,X⟩′⟨f1,Y†f2,Y⟩′∏Z≠X,YP0(Z¯Z¯)\displaystyle=-\langle f^{\dagger}_{2,X}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1,X}\rangle^{\prime}\langle f^{\dagger}_{1,Y}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2,Y}\rangle^{\prime}\prod_{Z\neq X,Y}P_{0}(\bar{Z}\bar{Z})
=−|ξ|2∏Z≠X,YP0(Z¯Z¯).\displaystyle=-|\xi|^{2}\prod_{Z\neq X,Y}P_{0}(\bar{Z}\bar{Z}). (64)

and eventually, we arrive at the

⟨𝒫12⟩\displaystyle\langle\mathcal{P}_{12}\rangle =∑X⟨X​X​|𝒫12|​X​X⟩+∑X≠Y⟨Y​X​|𝒫12|​X​Y⟩∑X=AF∑Y=AFP⁡(X​Y)\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{X}\langle XX|\mathcal{P}_{12}|XX\rangle+\sum_{X\neq Y}\langle YX|\mathcal{P}_{12}|XY\rangle}{\sum_{X=A}^{F}\sum_{Y=A}^{F}P(XY)}
=N​P​(A​A)+N⁡(N−1)​⟨B​A|𝒫12|A​B⟩N​P​(A​A)+N⁡(N−1)​P​(A​B)\displaystyle=\frac{NP(AA)+N(N-1)\langle BA|\mathcal{P}_{12}|AB\rangle}{NP(AA)+N(N-1)P(AB)}
=N​P0​(A​A)​P0​(B¯​B¯)−N⁡(N−1)​|ξ|2N​P0​(A​A)​P0​(B¯​B¯)+N⁡(N−1)​P0​(A​A¯)​P0​(B¯​B)\displaystyle=\frac{NP_{0}(AA)P_{0}(\bar{B}\bar{B})-N(N-1)|\xi|^{2}}{NP_{0}(AA)P_{0}(\bar{B}\bar{B})+N(N-1)P_{0}(A\bar{A})P_{0}(\bar{B}B)}
=(N−1)2−N2​(2−2​N+N3)​|ξ|2+N4​|ξ|4(N−1)2​N+(N−2)​N3​|ξ|2+N5​|ξ|4\displaystyle=\frac{(N-1)^{2}-N^{2}(2-2N+N^{3})|\xi|^{2}+N^{4}|\xi|^{4}}{(N-1)^{2}N+(N-2)N^{3}|\xi|^{2}+N^{5}|\xi|^{4}} (65)

This is the same result as Eq. (61) after we take Eq. (20) into account.

D.2 Projected mean field for 3-sites

Here, we extend the method to a triangle to consistently treat the three-site ring exchange. Using the same notation as above, the conditional expectation values are

⟨𝒫12⟩\displaystyle\langle\mathcal{P}_{12}\rangle =∑X,Y,Z⟨Y​X​Z|𝒫12|X​Y​Z⟩∑X,Y,ZP⁡(X​Y​Z)\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{X,Y,Z}\langle YXZ|\mathcal{P}_{12}|XYZ\rangle}{\sum_{X,Y,Z}P(XYZ)} (66a)
⟨𝒫123⟩\displaystyle\langle\mathcal{P}_{123}\rangle =∑X,Y,Z⟨Z​X​Y|𝒫123|X​Y​Z⟩∑X,Y,ZP⁡(X​Y​Z).\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{X,Y,Z}\langle ZXY|\mathcal{P}_{123}|XYZ\rangle}{\sum_{X,Y,Z}P(XYZ)}\;. (66b)

Assuming a homogenous state, |ξ1,2|=|ξ2,3|=|ξ3,1|=|ξ||\xi_{1,2}|=|\xi_{2,3}|=|\xi_{3,1}|=|\xi|, we can use the SU(NN) and geometrical symmetries of the system to write the denominator as

∑X,Y,ZP⁡(X​Y​Z)\displaystyle\sum_{X,Y,Z}P(XYZ) =N​P​(A​A​A)+3​N​(N−1)​P​(A​A​B)\displaystyle=NP(AAA)+3N(N-1)P(AAB)
+(N−2)​(N−1)​N​P​(A​B​C).\displaystyle\phantom{=}+(N-2)(N-1)NP(ABC). (67)

Regarding the numerator, the expectation values of the exchange operators are diagonal for certain configurations,

⟨A​A​A|𝒫12|A​A​A⟩\displaystyle\langle AAA|\mathcal{P}_{12}|AAA\rangle =P⁡(A​A​A),\displaystyle=P(AAA), (68a)
⟨A​A​B|𝒫12|A​A​B⟩\displaystyle\langle AAB|\mathcal{P}_{12}|AAB\rangle =P⁡(A​A​B),\displaystyle=P(AAB), (68b)
⟨A​A​A|𝒫123|A​A​A⟩\displaystyle\langle AAA|\mathcal{P}_{123}|AAA\rangle =P⁡(A​A​A),\displaystyle=P(AAA), (68c)
and for the off-diagonal, the
⟨B​A​A|𝒫123|A​A​B⟩\displaystyle\langle BAA|\mathcal{P}_{123}|AAB\rangle =⟨B​A​A|𝒫13|A​A​B⟩,\displaystyle=\langle BAA|\mathcal{P}_{13}|AAB\rangle, (68d)
⟨A​B​A|𝒫12|B​A​A⟩\displaystyle\langle ABA|\mathcal{P}_{12}|BAA\rangle =⟨B​A​A|𝒫12|A​B​A⟩¯]\displaystyle=\overline{\langle BAA|\mathcal{P}_{12}|ABA\rangle}] (68e)

holds. Again, the symmetries allow us to write

∑X,Y,Z\displaystyle\sum_{X,Y,Z} ⟨Y​X​Z|𝒫12|X​Y​Z⟩=N​P​(A​A​A)\displaystyle\langle YXZ|\mathcal{P}_{12}|XYZ\rangle=NP(AAA)
+N⁡(N−1)​P​(A​A​B)\displaystyle+N(N\!-\!1)P(AAB)
+N⁡(N−1)​(⟨B​A​A|𝒫12|A​B​A⟩+⟨A​B​A​|𝒫12|​B​A​A⟩)\displaystyle+N(N\!-\!1)\left(\langle BAA|\mathcal{P}_{12}|ABA\rangle+\langle ABA|\mathcal{P}_{12}|BAA\rangle\right)
+(N−2)​(N−1)​⟨B​A​C|𝒫12|A​B​C⟩,\displaystyle+(N\!-\!2)(N\!-\!1)\langle BAC|\mathcal{P}_{12}|ABC\rangle\,, (69a)
∑X,Y,Z\displaystyle\sum_{X,Y,Z} ⟨Z​X​Y|𝒫123|X​Y​Z⟩=N​P​(A​A​A)\displaystyle\langle ZXY|\mathcal{P}_{123}|XYZ\rangle=NP(AAA)
+3​N​(N−1)​⟨A​B​A|𝒫12|B​A​A⟩\displaystyle+3N(N\!-\!1)\langle ABA|\mathcal{P}_{12}|BAA\rangle
+(N−2)​(N−1)​N​⟨C​A​B|𝒫123|A​B​C⟩.\displaystyle+(N\!-\!2)(N\!-\!1)N\langle CAB|\mathcal{P}_{123}|ABC\rangle\,. (69b)

where the probabilities are

P⁡(A​A​A)=P0​(A​A​A)​∏X≠AP0​(X¯​X¯​X¯)P(AAA)=P_{0}(AAA)\prod_{X\neq A}P_{0}(\bar{X}\bar{X}\bar{X}) (70a)
P⁡(A​A​B)=P0​(A​A​A¯)​P0​(B¯​B¯​B)​∏X≠A,BP0​(X¯​X¯​X¯)P(AAB)=P_{0}(AA\bar{A})P_{0}(\bar{B}\bar{B}B)\prod_{X\neq A,B}P_{0}(\bar{X}\bar{X}\bar{X}) (70b)
P⁡(A​B​C)=P0​(A​A¯​A¯)​P0​(B¯​B​B¯)​P0​(C¯​C¯​C)×∏X≠A,B,CP0​(X¯​X¯​X¯)P(ABC)=P_{0}(A\bar{A}\bar{A})P_{0}(\bar{B}B\bar{B})P_{0}(\bar{C}\bar{C}C)\\ \times\prod_{X\neq A,B,C}P_{0}(\bar{X}\bar{X}\bar{X}) (70c)
⟨B​A​A|𝒫12|A​B​A⟩=−⟨f2,A†​f3,A†​f3,A​f1,A⟩′​⟨f1,B†​f2,B⟩′×∏X≠A,BP0​(X¯​X¯​X¯),\langle BAA|\mathcal{P}_{12}|ABA\rangle=-\langle f^{\dagger}_{2,A}f^{\dagger}_{3,A}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{3,A}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1,A}\rangle^{\prime}\langle f^{\dagger}_{1,B}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2,B}\rangle^{\prime}\\ \times\prod_{X\neq A,B}P_{0}(\bar{X}\bar{X}\bar{X})\,, (70d)
⟨B​A​C|𝒫12|A​B​C⟩=−⟨f2,A†​f1,A⟩′​⟨f1,B†​f2,B⟩′​P0​(C¯​C¯​C)×∏X≠A,B,CP0​(X¯​X¯​X¯),\langle BAC|\mathcal{P}_{12}|ABC\rangle=-\langle f^{\dagger}_{2,A}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1,A}\rangle^{\prime}\langle f^{\dagger}_{1,B}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2,B}\rangle^{\prime}P_{0}(\bar{C}\bar{C}C)\\ \times\prod_{X\neq A,B,C}P_{0}(\bar{X}\bar{X}\bar{X})\,, (70e)
⟨C​A​B|𝒫123|A​B​C⟩=⟨f2,A†​f1,A⟩′​⟨f3,B†​f2,B⟩′×⟨f1,C†​f3,C⟩′​∏X≠A,B,CP0​(X¯​X¯​X¯).\langle CAB|\mathcal{P}_{123}|ABC\rangle=\langle f^{\dagger}_{2,A}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1,A}\rangle^{\prime}\langle f^{\dagger}_{3,B}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2,B}\rangle^{\prime}\\ \times\langle f^{\dagger}_{1,C}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{3,C}\rangle^{\prime}\prod_{X\neq A,B,C}P_{0}(\bar{X}\bar{X}\bar{X})\,. (70f)

Here again, we can use Wick’s theorem to calculate the probabilities in the Fermi-sea of free fermions as

P0​(X​X​X)\displaystyle P_{0}(XXX) =⟨n1,X​n2,X​n3,X⟩′=|ν1Xξ1,2Xξ1,3Xξ2,1Xν2Xξ2,3Xξ3,1Xξ3,2Xν3X|,\displaystyle=\langle n_{1,X}n_{2,X}n_{3,X}\rangle^{\prime}=\begin{vmatrix}\nu^{X}_{1}&\xi^{X}_{1,2}&\xi^{X}_{1,3}\\ \xi^{X}_{2,1}&\nu^{X}_{2}&\xi^{X}_{2,3}\\ \xi^{X}_{3,1}&\xi^{X}_{3,2}&\nu^{X}_{3}\\ \end{vmatrix}\,, (71a)
P0​(X​X​X¯)\displaystyle P_{0}(XX\bar{X}) =⟨n1,X​n2,X​n¯3,X⟩′=|ν1Xξ1,2X−ξ1,3Xξ2,1Xν2X−ξ2,3Xξ3,1Xξ3,2X1−ν3X|\displaystyle=\langle n_{1,X}n_{2,X}\bar{n}_{3,X}\rangle^{\prime}=\begin{vmatrix}\nu^{X}_{1}&\xi^{X}_{1,2}&-\xi^{X}_{1,3}\\ \xi^{X}_{2,1}&\nu^{X}_{2}&-\xi^{X}_{2,3}\\ \xi^{X}_{3,1}&\xi^{X}_{3,2}&1-\nu^{X}_{3}\\ \end{vmatrix} (71b)
P0​(X​X¯​X¯)\displaystyle P_{0}(X\bar{X}\bar{X}) =⟨n1,X​n¯2,X​n¯3,X⟩′=|ν1X−ξ1,2X−ξ1,3Xξ2,1X1−ν2X−ξ2,3Xξ3,1X−ξ3,2X1−ν3X|,\displaystyle=\langle n_{1,X}\bar{n}_{2,X}\bar{n}_{3,X}\rangle^{\prime}=\begin{vmatrix}\nu^{X}_{1}&-\xi^{X}_{1,2}&-\xi^{X}_{1,3}\\ \xi^{X}_{2,1}&1-\nu^{X}_{2}&-\xi^{X}_{2,3}\\ \xi^{X}_{3,1}&-\xi^{X}_{3,2}&1-\nu^{X}_{3}\\ \end{vmatrix}\,, (71c)
P0​(X¯​X¯​X¯)\displaystyle P_{0}(\bar{X}\bar{X}\bar{X}) =⟨n¯1,X​n¯2,X​n¯3,X⟩′=|1−ν1X−ξ1,2X−ξ1,3X−ξ2,1X1−ν2X−ξ2,3X−ξ3,1X−ξ3,2X1−ν3X|,\displaystyle=\langle\bar{n}_{1,X}\bar{n}_{2,X}\bar{n}_{3,X}\rangle^{\prime}=\begin{vmatrix}1-\nu^{X}_{1}&-\xi^{X}_{1,2}&-\xi^{X}_{1,3}\\ -\xi^{X}_{2,1}&1-\nu^{X}_{2}&-\xi^{X}_{2,3}\\ -\xi^{X}_{3,1}&-\xi^{X}_{3,2}&1-\nu^{X}_{3}\\ \end{vmatrix}\,, (71d)
and the off-diagonal expectation values
⟨f2,X†​f3,X†​f3,X​f1,X⟩′\displaystyle\langle f^{\dagger}_{2,X}f^{\dagger}_{3,X}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{3,X}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1,X}\rangle^{\prime} =|ξ2,1Xξ2,3Xξ3,1Xν3X|\displaystyle=\begin{vmatrix}\xi^{X}_{2,1}&\xi^{X}_{2,3}\\ \xi^{X}_{3,1}&\nu^{X}_{3}\\ \end{vmatrix} (71e)

Collecting all the terms together and using computer algebra, we arrive at the following expressions:

⟨𝒫12⟩\displaystyle\langle\mathcal{P}_{12}\rangle =1N−(N2−1)​N2​Θ12Σ,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}-(N^{2}-1)N^{2}\frac{\Theta_{12}}{\Sigma}\,, (72)
⟨𝒫123+𝒫132⟩\displaystyle\langle\mathcal{P}_{123}+\mathcal{P}_{132}\rangle =2N2−(N2−1)​N​Θ123+132Σ,\displaystyle=\frac{2}{N^{2}}-(N^{2}-1)N\frac{\Theta_{123+132}}{\Sigma}\,, (73)

where

Σ=1−6N−3[3ξ2−5]N2+[6ξ3cosϕ△+39ξ2−20]N3+[27ξ4−20ξ3cosϕ△−66ξ2+15]N4−6[6ξ5cosϕ△+13ξ4−4ξ3cosϕ△−9ξ2+1]N5+[6ξ6cos2ϕ△−21ξ6+66ξ5cosϕ△+81ξ4−12ξ3cosϕ△−21ξ2+1]N6+ξ2[54ξ5cosϕ△−4ξ4cos2ϕ△+57ξ4−36ξ3cosϕ△−36ξ2+2ξcosϕ△+3]N7−6ξ4[3ξ4cos2ϕ△+3ξ4+13ξ3cosϕ△+7ξ2−ξcosϕ△−1]N82ξ6[3ξ3cosϕ△+ξ3cos3ϕ△+6ξ2cos2ϕ△+6ξ2+12ξcosϕ△+4]N9,\Sigma=1-6N-3\left[3\xi^{2}-5\right]N^{2}+\left[6\xi^{3}\cos\phi_{\triangle}+39\xi^{2}-20\right]N^{3}+\left[27\xi^{4}-20\xi^{3}\cos\phi_{\triangle}-66\xi^{2}+15\right]N^{4}\\ -6\left[6\xi^{5}\cos\phi_{\triangle}+13\xi^{4}-4\xi^{3}\cos\phi_{\triangle}-9\xi^{2}+1\right]N^{5}\\ +\left[6\xi^{6}\cos 2\phi_{\triangle}-21\xi^{6}+66\xi^{5}\cos\phi_{\triangle}+81\xi^{4}-12\xi^{3}\cos\phi_{\triangle}-21\xi^{2}+1\right]N^{6}\\ +\xi^{2}\left[54\xi^{5}\cos\phi_{\triangle}-4\xi^{4}\cos 2\phi_{\triangle}+57\xi^{4}-36\xi^{3}\cos\phi_{\triangle}-36\xi^{2}+2\xi\cos\phi_{\triangle}+3\right]N^{7}\\ -6\xi^{4}\left[3\xi^{4}\cos 2\phi_{\triangle}+3\xi^{4}+13\xi^{3}\cos\phi_{\triangle}+7\xi^{2}-\xi\cos\phi_{\triangle}-1\right]N^{8}\\ 2\xi^{6}\left[3\xi^{3}\cos\phi_{\triangle}+\xi^{3}\cos 3\phi_{\triangle}+6\xi^{2}\cos 2\phi_{\triangle}+6\xi^{2}+12\xi\cos\phi_{\triangle}+4\right]N^{9}\,, (74)

Appendix E Lower bound on the ground state energy

In this section we present a modification of Anderson’s method [4, 50, *NishimoriOzekiJPSJ1989, *Tarrach, 83] to give a lower bound on the ground state energy EGSE_{\text{GS}} of the Hamiltonian (19) with nearest neighbor exchanges only,

ℋ=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩𝒫i,j.\mathcal{H}=J_{1}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\mathcal{P}_{i,j}. (77)

To this end, we write the ℋ\mathcal{H} as a sum of sub-Hamiltonians ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime},

ℋ=∑iℋi′,\mathcal{H}=\sum_{i}\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{i}, (78)

where ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} is defined on a 12-site cluster drawn in Fig. 19, and the index ii runs over every hexagon of the kagome lattice. We assume ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} to manifest the D6D_{6} point group of the Kagome lattice, so that

ℋi′=g​ℋ0′​g−1,\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{i}=g\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{0}g^{-1}, (79)

where gg is an element of the D6⊗TD_{6}\otimes T wallpaper group [76]. In other words, the gg translates ℋ0′\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{0} into ℋi′\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{i} if it contains a translation operator. The nearest neighbor bonds shown in Fig. 19(a) form a David star, in which Eq. (79) allows for two different exchanges, J1′J_{1}^{\prime} and J1′′J_{1}^{\prime\prime}. Since the index ii in Eq. (78) runs over every hexagon, these David stars overlap, so that every nearest neighbor bond is a part of three overlapping ℋi′\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{i}, once with exchange J1′′J_{1}^{\prime\prime} and twice with J1′J_{1}^{\prime}. Therefore, Eqs. (77) and (78) gives the constraint

J1=J1′′+2​J1′.J_{1}=J^{\prime\prime}_{1}+2J^{\prime}_{1}\;. (80)

We can also include higher-distance exchanges in ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} even though they do not appear in the Hamiltonian ℋ\mathcal{H} [i.e., J2=0J_{2}=0 in Eq. (19)]. Eq. (79) allows for two different next-nearest neighbor exchanges J2′J_{2}^{\prime} and J2′′J_{2}^{\prime\prime} in ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime}, shown in Fig. 19(b). Since every next-nearest neighbor bond is a part of two different ℋi′\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{i}, once with exchange J2′J^{\prime}_{2} and once with J2′′J^{\prime\prime}_{2}, from Eq. (78) we get the condition

0=J2=J2′+J2′′0=J_{2}=J^{\prime}_{2}+J^{\prime\prime}_{2} (81)

constraint. For the ground state energy per site, the

EGSNs≥EGS′3\frac{E_{\text{GS}}}{N_{s}}\geq\frac{E^{\prime}_{\text{GS}}}{3} (82)

holds, where EGS′E^{\prime}_{\text{GS}} is the ground state energy of the 12-site Hamiltonian ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} with parameters subject to constraints Eqs. (80) and (81). The factor 1/3 comes from having Ns/3N_{s}/3 such clusters (Ns/3N_{s}/3 is the number of hexagons) in an NsN_{s} site lattice. Thus, the maximal EGS′E^{\prime}_{\text{GS}}, as we vary J1′J^{\prime}_{1} and J2′J^{\prime}_{2}, gives a lower bound energy ELBE_{\text{LB}} for the ℋ\mathcal{H} Heisenberg model in the thermodynamic limit:

ELB=13​maxJ1′,J2′​EGS′​(J1′,J2′).E_{\text{LB}}=\frac{1}{3}\max_{J^{\prime}_{1},J^{\prime}_{2}}E^{\prime}_{\text{GS}}(J^{\prime}_{1},J^{\prime}_{2}). (83)

Using the Lánczos method, we diagonalized the 12-site Hamiltonian for J1=1J_{1}=1 and J2=0J_{2}=0 in the Hilbert subspace where each of the six flavors occupies two sites and plot EGS′​(J1′,J2′)/3E^{\prime}_{\text{GS}}(J^{\prime}_{1},J^{\prime}_{2})/3 in Fig 20(a). Applying the Nelder-Mead method, the maximum ground state energy is at J1′=0.2606476​(0)J_{1}^{\prime}=0.2606476(0), J1′′=0.4787048​(0)J^{\prime\prime}_{1}=0.4787048(0) and J2′=−J2′′=0.1211317​(1)J_{2}^{\prime}=-J_{2}^{\prime\prime}=0.1211317(1), and the the spectrum of the Hamiltonian (77) is bounded from below by the per-site energy

ELB=−1.557157​(6)​J1.E_{\text{LB}}=-1.557157(6)J_{1}. (84)

The lower bound for the expectation value of the permutation operator 𝒫1st\mathcal{P}_{\text{1st}} between nearest neighbors is half of the energy (there are two bonds for each site in the kagome lattice), ⟨𝒫1st⟩≥−0.778579\langle\mathcal{P}_{\text{1st}}\rangle\geq-0.778579. It appears that the optimal energy is reached where the exchanges at the boundary are weaker than in the center, thus reducing the boundary effects.

Excluding the second neighbor exchanges from ℋ′\mathcal{H^{\prime}} (i.e. J2′=J2′′=0J_{2}^{\prime}=J_{2}^{\prime\prime}=0), the lower bound is ELB=−1.596933​(7)E_{\text{LB}}=-1.596933(7), reached for the J1′=(1−J1′′)/2=0.100148​(3)J_{1}^{\prime}=(1-J_{1}^{\prime\prime})/2=0.100148(3) parameter value [see Fig. 20(b)]. For a cluster with uniform first neighbor exchanges J1′=J1′′=1/3J^{\prime}_{1}=J^{\prime\prime}_{1}=1/3 [green vertical line in Fig. 20(b)] EGS′=−5.262256​(5)E^{\prime}_{\text{GS}}=-5.262256(5) and the estimated lower bound is considerably worse, ELB=−1.754085​(5)​J1E_{\text{LB}}=-1.754085(5)J_{1}. The energy is maximal at the cusp of the ground state energy plot, indicating a level crossing. Indeed, the ground state wave function has different parity under reflections.

We can also use the 12-site cluster with J1′=J1′′=1J^{\prime}_{1}=J^{\prime\prime}_{1}=1 to get a variational estimate (upper bound) for the energy [83]. The variational wave function is a product of the 12-site wave functions covering the lattice with David stars (see Fig. 21), the energy per site is simply the energy of the 12-site cluster plus the expectation values of the 𝒫\mathcal{P} exchange between the David stars. Since the ground state is a singlet, from Eq. (20) we get the ⟨𝒫1st⟩=J1/6\langle\mathcal{P}_{\text{1st}}\rangle=J_{1}/6 for the latter. The energy of the 12-site unit cell is then the energy of the decoupled David-star (−3×5.262256(5)=−15.78677(2)-3\times 5.262256(5)=-15.78677(2), see the paragraph above) plus the energy J1J_{1} coming from the bonds connecting the clusters (there are six bonds in the unit cell, each having J1/6J_{1}/6), so the upper bound per site is EUB=[−15.78677​(2)+1]​J1/12=−1.232230​(8)​J1E_{\text{UB}}=[-15.78677(2)+1]J_{1}/12=-1.232230(8)J_{1}. Putting the lower and the upper bound together, the 12-site cluster provides

−0.778579≤⟨𝒫1st⟩≤−0.616115.-0.778579\leq\langle\mathcal{P}_{\text{1st}}\rangle\leq-0.616115. (85)

The VMC energy of the π\pi-flux state, ⟨𝒫1st⟩VMC=−0.6885\langle\mathcal{P}_{\text{1st}}\rangle_{\text{VMC}}=-0.6885, is roughly in the middle of this interval. Alternatively, for the nearest neighbor correlations, we get

−0.472623≤⟨𝐓1⋅𝐓2⟩≤−0.391391.-0.472623\leq\langle\mathbf{T}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{2}\rangle\leq-0.391391. (86)

Appendix F The instability of the Ferromagnetic phase

In this section, we calculate the stability of the ferromagnetic state in the SU(6) Heisenberg model described by the Hamiltonian  (19). The ferromagnet is a lattice-symmetric state, which spontaneously breaks the internal SU(6) symmetry, where both the two-site and the three-site permutations act trivially with eigenvalues +1+1. Hence, the ground state energy per site is

eFM=2​J1+2​J2+4​K/3.e_{\text{FM}}=2J_{1}+2J_{2}+4K/3. (87)

It is represented by the Young tableau having NsN_{s} boxes in a single row.

F.1 Single-magnon instability

To determine the phase boundary of the ferromagnetic state, we first calculate the dispersion of a single magnon (two-magnon instabilities are discussed in the next section). By this, we mean configurations with identical flavors (say A) on all sites except one (say B), i.e., we flip an A spin into B. The Hamiltonian then hops the BB flavor to neighboring sites, endowing it with a dispersion determined by the eigenvalues of the three-by-three matrix

ℋ1​m=2​(J1+K)​(−2cos⁡q12cos⁡q31cos⁡q12−2cos⁡q23cos⁡q31cos⁡q23−2)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{1m}=2(J_{1}+K)\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}-2&\cos q_{12}&\cos q_{31}\\ \cos q_{12}&-2&\cos q_{23}\\ \cos q_{31}&\cos q_{23}&-2\\ \end{array}\right)
+2​J2​(−2cos⁡(q23−q31)cos⁡(q12−q23)cos⁡(q23−q31)−2cos⁡(q31−q12)cos⁡(q12−q23)cos⁡(q31−q12)−2)\displaystyle+2J_{2}\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}-2&\cos(q_{23}\!-\!q_{31})&\cos(q_{12}\!-\!q_{23})\\ \cos(q_{23}\!-\!q_{31})&-2&\cos(q_{31}\!-\!q_{12})\\ \cos(q_{12}\!-\!q_{23})&\cos(q_{31}\!-\!q_{12})&-2\\ \end{array}\right)

in reciprocal space, where the energy is measured from the energy of the ferromagnetic state and qi​j=𝐪⋅𝜹i​jq_{ij}=\mathbf{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\delta}_{ij}, where 𝐪=(qx,qy)\mathbf{q}=(q_{x},q_{y}) is the momentum of the magnon and

𝜹12\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\delta}_{12} =𝐚22−𝐚12=(−14,34),\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbf{a}_{2}}{2}-\frac{\mathbf{a}_{1}}{2}=\left(-\frac{1}{4},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right),
𝜹31\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\delta}_{31} =−𝐚22=(−14,−34),\displaystyle=-\frac{\mathbf{a}_{2}}{2}=\left(-\frac{1}{4},-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right), (94)
𝜹23\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\delta}_{23} =𝐚12=(12,0)\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbf{a}_{1}}{2}=\left(\frac{1}{2},0\right)

are lattice unit vectors. The Hamiltonian (F.1) describes three magnon branches measured from the energy of the ferromagnetic state. Since the J1J_{1} and KK appear as a combination J1+KJ_{1}+K in the matrix above, the dispersion depends only on two free parameters, J1+KJ_{1}+K and J2J_{2}. It turns out that the lowest magnon band is flat for two cases: (i) the kagome lattice with nearest neighbor exchanges when J2=0J_{2}=0 and J1+K>0J_{1}+K>0 [the green line in Fig. (22)]; (ii) J1+K=0J_{1}+K=0 and J2>0J_{2}>0 [the magenta line in Fig. (22)] that describes three intercalating decoupled kagome lattices. The extremal values of the dispersions appear at the symmetric points in the Brillouin zone. The one-magnon energies are εM=−6​(J1+K)−2​J2\varepsilon_{M}=-6(J_{1}+K)-2J_{2}, −2​(J1+K)−6​J2-2(J_{1}+K)-6J_{2}, and −4​(J1+K)−4​J2-4(J_{1}+K)-4J_{2} at the 𝐪M=(0,2​π/3)\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{M}}=(0,2\pi/\sqrt{3}) and the symmetry-related ”M” points, εK=−6​(J1+K)\varepsilon_{K}=-6(J_{1}+K) and the two-fold degenerate −3​(J1+K)−6​J2-3(J_{1}+K)-6J_{2} at the 𝐪K=(±4π/3,0)\mathbf{q}_{\text{K}}=(\pm 4\pi/3,0) ”K” points, and εΓ=−6​(J1+K)−6​J2\varepsilon_{\Gamma}=-6(J_{1}+K)-6J_{2} (two-fold degenerate) and 00 at the Γ\Gamma point (𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0).

When the one-magnon dispersion becomes negative, we do not need to invest energy to reverse a spin, and the ferromagnetic state is no longer the ground state. Examining the extremal values at the high symmetry points, we find that the dispersion becomes negative at the M\mathrm{M} point when J1+K=−3​J2>0J_{1}+K=-3J_{2}>0 and at the K point when J1+K=0J_{1}+K=0 and J2≤0J_{2}\leq 0. These instabilities are shown as black lines in Fig. 22, and the ferromagnet is stable against a single spin flip in the white region given by J1+K+3​J2<0J_{1}+K+3J_{2}<0 and J1+K<0J_{1}+K<0.

F.2 Instability due to two-magnon bound states

In addition, we also examined the stability of the ferromagnetic state against the formation of bound pairs of magnons. To this end, we considered a two-magnon excitation of the ferromagnetic state, where two spins are flipped to different flavors. The two-magnon calculation reveals whether the interaction between the magnons is attractive and leads to a bound state, in which case the boundary of the ferromagnetic phase shrinks further. We followed the calculations in Ref. 86 for the SU(3) Heisenberg model and Refs. 84, 28 for the SU(2) case.

Starting from the highest weight state of the fully symmetrical irreducible representation, |A​A​…​A⟩|AA\dots A\rangle, as a vacuum, the two-magnon wave function is

Ψ=∑i,j∈Λci,j​|A​…​A​Bi​A​…​A​Cj​A​…​A⟩.\Psi=\sum_{i,j\in\Lambda}c_{i,j}|A\dots AB_{i}A\dots AC_{j}A\dots A\rangle\;. (95)

The dimension of the Hilbert space spanned by |A​…​A​Bi​A​…​A​Cj​A​…​A⟩|A\dots AB_{i}A\dots AC_{j}A\dots A\rangle basis is Ns​(Ns−1)N_{s}(N_{s}-1), as i=1,…,Nsi=1,\dots,N_{s} and j=1,…,Nsj=1,\dots,N_{s}, but the BB and CC cannot occupy the same site (i≠ji\neq j). Within these states, we will find Ns−1N_{s}-1 states that belong to the 𝐝=(Ns−1)​(Ns+1)\mathbf{d}=(N_{s}-1)(N_{s}+1) dimensional Young diagram with (Ns−2,1,0,0,0)(N_{s}-2,1,0,0,0) Dynkin label, which are just rotated single-magnon states, and a state with zero energy which belongs to the 𝐝=(Ns+1)​(Ns+2)/2\mathbf{d}=(N_{s}+1)(N_{s}+2)/2 dimensional fully symmetrical irreducible representation of the ferromagnetic state. But also new irreducible representations appear, denoted by the (Ns−4,2,0,0,)(N_{s}-4,2,0,0,) and (Ns−3,0,1,0,0)(N_{s}-3,0,1,0,0) Young diagrams (see Fig. 23).

We diagonalized the Hamiltonian matrix for up to 108-site clusters numerically (in principle, being a two-body problem, it can be solved analytically, but the expressions would be pretty cumbersome). Using the Casimir operator, we separated the energies of the (Ns−4,2,0,0,0)(N_{s}-4,2,0,0,0) and (Ns−3,0,1,0,0)(N_{s}-3,0,1,0,0) irreducible representations. The (Ns−4,2,0,0,0)(N_{s}-4,2,0,0,0) state also appears in the SU(2) case since the configurations with two BB type spins (instead of BB and CC) are members of the multiplet. However, the (Ns−3,0,1,0,0)(N_{s}-3,0,1,0,0) is unique to the SU(N) models with N≥3N\geq 3. We found that there are bound pairs in the (Ns−3,0,1,0,0)(N_{s}-3,0,1,0,0) irreducible representation in the region we investigated in Fig. 22. The number of bound pairs is 2​Ns/32N_{s}/3, which is also the number of triangles– for substantial ring exchange KK with a negative sign, the BB and CC spins are localized on a triangle. In the momentum space, two bound pairs form two bands for each momentum. The lowest energy bound state is at the Γ\Gamma point in the Brillouin zone, but it can have different point group symmetry. The solid red and blue curves in Fig. 22 show when these bound states start to have lower energy from the ferromagnet, leading to the instability of the ferromagnet. For the J2=0J_{2}=0 value, the bound state energy becomes negative for K/J1>−2.7532K/J_{1}>-2.7532 [86]. We did not examine whether the interaction between the bound pairs is repulsive or attractive (in which case the ferromagnet region would shrink further).

The solution with negative signs determines the singular point discussed in Sec. V.2.1: Each David star has six banana-shaped localized orbitals, giving rise to a six-fold degenerate flat band in the momentum space.

For the coupled David stars we can linearly combine the banana-shaped states into a state shown in Fig. 24(b) that encompass two hexagons and zero flux, where the alternating amplitudes uu and −u-u ensures the locality at the isosceles triangles, and Eqs. (96) modify to include the effect of a finite t△t_{\triangle} hopping,

Unlike the flat bands for the 00-flux kagome lattice [9], these flat bands are non-topological (they form a set of N⎔=Ns/3N_{\hexagon}=N_{s}/3 linearly independent states, where N⎔N_{\hexagon} is the number of hexagons).
